query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Severe plastic deformation that refines the grain size of high-entropy alloy coatings to below approximately 20 nm switches the dominant deformation mechanism from dislocation‐mediated plasticity to grain boundary‐mediated sliding, resulting in an adaptive amorphous–crystalline surface layer that lowers shear strength and friction, thereby enhancing wear resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloy protective coating with a baseline microstructure characterized by larger, approximately 100-nm-class grains that primarily deform by dislocation activity under wear.
generation.intervention: Apply severe plastic deformation (or similar grain refinement techniques) to reduce the grain size in the coating to below ~20 nm.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests under controlled normal loads and sliding speeds, where the deformation is confined to a thin surface layer.
generation.structural_mediator: A significantly increased density of grain boundaries in the refined surface layer, which facilitates grain boundary sliding and may promote the formation of an amorphous–crystalline nanocomposite protective layer.
generation.mechanism: With grain sizes below ~20 nm, conventional dislocation-mediated plasticity is suppressed. The high density of nanograin boundaries enhances grain boundary sliding, leading to dynamic softening (i.e., inverse Hall–Petch behavior). This process also facilitates the formation of an adaptive surface layer (possibly incorporating tribo-oxidized structures) that reduces the local shear strength and friction during wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under sliding wear conditions, coatings with a refined grain structure (<20 nm) will exhibit lower friction coefficients and reduced wear rates compared to the baseline coating. The change should be evident during initial sliding cycles, with microstructural analysis (e.g., TEM) revealing enhanced grain boundary sliding features and the formation of an adaptive nanocomposite layer.
generation.baseline: A similar high-entropy alloy coating processed without the severe plastic deformation, retaining larger grain sizes (>~100 nm) where dislocation motion is the dominant deformation mechanism.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis should hold under wear conditions where the plastic deformation is localized near the surface (typically within the first micrometer) and at normal loads/sliding speeds that induce severe plastic deformation without causing catastrophic failure or oxidation-dominated wear regimes.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative reduction in friction coefficient and wear rate is uncertain and may vary with alloy composition and wear test parameters. The interplay between grain boundary sliding and other potential surface modifications (e.g., oxide layer formation) may also influence the observed effects.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy coatings: one set processed with severe plastic deformation to achieve grain sizes below 20 nm and a control set with the as-deposited, coarser microstructure. Subject both sets to identical sliding wear tests under controlled conditions (normal loads and sliding speeds) while monitoring the wear track evolution.
measurements: Wear rate (e.g., volume loss per cycle)
Post-test microstructural characterization (TEM, STEM) to assess grain size and the presence of an amorphous–crystalline surface layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the refined coatings (grain size <20 nm) do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in friction and wear rate compared to the baseline or if microstructural analysis fails to reveal evidence of enhanced grain boundary sliding and adaptive surface layer formation, then the hypothesis would be refuted.

The Hall-Petch equation, σy=σ0+k⋅d−1/2, is fit to the Luo data only, and agrees reasonably well with the nano-grained estimate from Schuh, et al.. This is well described by a recently proposed predictive model that explains the low shear strength and friction coefficients of bare metals and alloys. cited_evidence.text: To understand the wear mechanism, we investigated the structures of the wear surfaces at atomic scale using TEM and aberration-corrected scanning TEM (STEM). In the worn TiNbZr alloy, the original columnar grains have been refined into ~10-nm-diameter globular grains within ~1 μm depth from the surface (Fig. 2c2–c4). Grain refinement is a common phenomenon for crystalline metals exposed to wear. This effect is attributed to the high density of dislocations forming sub-grain boundaries to reduce their distortion energy. The wear surface of the (TiNbZr)90Ag10 alloy shows a multilayer structure comprising regions of a ~20-nm-thick nanocrystalline phase separated by ~5-nm-thick amorphous interfaces (Supplementary Fig. 5). In the worn (TiNbZr)75Ag25 alloy, the nanograins are slightly curved at a depth of 1.6–3.4 μm below the surface, and globular grains with ~30 nm diameter are observed at 1.6 μm depth from the surface (Fig. 2d2). Different from the two reference alloys, a ~400-nm-thick amorphous surface layer, in which nanocrystals with diameters from 5 nm to 20 nm are embedded, is found in the worn (TiNbZr)75Ag25 alloy (Fig. 2d3).
